items.hint: Work from the inside out: the number $4$ goes into $g$ first, and whatever comes out is the input for $f$.
worked: That output becomes the input for $f$: $f(7)=2(7)+1=14+1$.

items.stem: Let $f(x)=x^{2}$ and $g(x)=x+3$. Write $(f\circ g)(x)$ as a simplified polynomial.
items.hint: $(f\circ g)(x)$ means $f(g(x))$, so the entire expression $x+3$ takes the place of $x$ inside $f$.
worked: Substitute the whole input into the squaring rule: $f(x+3)=(x+3)^{2}$.

items.stem: Let $f(x)=4-x$ and $g(x)=2x-7$. A student writes $(f\circ g)(x)=4-2x-7=-2x-3$. Her substitution was right and her sign step was wrong. What is the correct simplified form of $(f\circ g)(x)$?
items.hint: Put all of $g(x)$ inside parentheses before you subtract it, then hand the minus sign to every term in those parentheses.
worked: Distribute the negative to both terms: $4-2x+7$. The student stopped after the first term.

items.stem: Let $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ and $g(x)=x-9$. Exactly one statement below is true. Which one?
items.hint: Build the composite by substituting $g(x)$ into $f$ first, then ask which inputs keep the quantity under the radical from going negative.
worked: $(f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))=f(x-9)$, so the whole of $x-9$ goes under the radical: $\sqrt{x-9}$.
A square root needs a non-negative radicand, so $x-9\ge 0$.
That gives $x\ge 9$, so the composite is $\sqrt{x-9}$ with domain $x\ge 9$.

items.stem: Let $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-2}$ and $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$. State the domain of $(f\circ g)(x)$.
items.hint: A number must survive two tests: the inner function has to accept it, and the inner function's output has to be legal for the outer function. Simplifying first can hide the first test.
worked: First test: $g(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}$ is undefined at $x=0$, so $x\ne 0$.
Second test: $f$ is undefined when its input is $2$, so we need $\dfrac{1}{x}\ne 2$, which gives $x\ne\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Simplifying gives $(f\circ g)(x)=\dfrac{x}{1-2x}$, which shows only $x\ne\dfrac{1}{2}$, so the $x\ne 0$ restriction must be carried over from step one.
Domain: all real numbers except $x=0$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
